what_it_does: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a technique for rendering photorealistic 3D scenes: instead of storing a scene as triangles, it stores it as millions of fuzzy 3D blobs (Gaussians), each with a position, shape, colour, and opacity, which are then 'splat' projected onto the screen and blended together. This is computationally expensive and too slow for real-time use on the small, power-limited GPUs found in phones or headsets. Prior solutions built entirely new custom chips (dedicated accelerators), which are costly to design and integrate. GauRast instead notices that 3DGS shares structure with conventional triangle rasterization — the existing GPU pipeline for drawing triangles — and proposes modest modifications to that already-present rasterizer hardware to also handle Gaussian splat operations and blending, avoiding the cost of a separate chip. The novelty is reusing existing GPU silicon rather than adding new hardware, which is more practical for manufacturers already shipping graphics-capable chips.
